frameworks.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
frameworks.hook: The common language for cyber risk, from boardroom to SOC.
frameworks.summary: NIST's voluntary framework organizes cybersecurity outcomes into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Profiles and tiers turn risk appetite into a prioritized, sector-neutral programme that boards and engineers can both use.
keyPoints: Six functions replace the original five, with Govern now explicit and central.
Organizational profiles compare current and target outcomes; community profiles tailor the model to a sector or mission.
Implementation tiers describe the rigor of risk governance, not a certification or a maturity score.
Informative references map outcomes to NIST SP 800-53, ISO/IEC 27001, CIS Controls and other standards.
Small-business quick starts and self-assessment tools make adoption practical beyond large enterprises.
Use is voluntary in the US, but regulators, insurers and boards increasingly treat it as a shared lens.
crownJewels: Critical products, services and the dependencies that keep them running.
Asset, identity and data inventories that make risk visible and measurable.
Risk appetite, tolerances and named executive accountability.
Detection, response and recovery capability for high-impact scenarios.
Supply-chain and third-party risk visibility.
clientUse: Open an engagement by mapping what the client already does to the six functions.
Compare current and target profiles to build a board-ready roadmap and budget case.
Use the tiers to describe governance rigor without implying certification.
Adopt the framework as the spine for a multi-standard compliance programme.

frameworks.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
frameworks.hook: The control catalogue behind FedRAMP, CMMC and much of US federal security.
frameworks.summary: SP 800-53 is NIST's deep catalogue of security and privacy controls for federal systems and the organizations that serve them. Baselines and overlays let teams tailor a defensible control set without starting from a blank page.
keyPoints: Twenty control families span access, audit, configuration, incident response, supply chain and privacy.
SP 800-53B provides low, moderate, high and privacy baselines for different impact levels.
Overlays adapt the catalogue to cloud, OT, mobile, PCI and other specialized environments.
SP 800-53A defines assessment procedures; OSCAL provides machine-readable control content.
Controls are selected through the RMF, then implemented, assessed, authorized and monitored.
Control enhancements allow teams to dial assurance up for high-value systems.
crownJewels: High-impact systems and the data they process, especially PII and CUI.
Privileged and service accounts with elevated access.
Audit logs and other evidence needed to prove control operation.
Cryptographic keys, trust stores and certificate authorities.
Supplier and third-party connections that cross the authorization boundary.
clientUse: Build a control matrix that maps existing evidence to the selected baseline.
Tailor controls and document inherited controls from cloud or shared-service providers.
Use 800-53A procedures to design an assessment plan instead of a document dump.
Prepare authorization packages and continuous-monitoring cadence for federal work.

frameworks.title: NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF)
frameworks.hook: A seven-step discipline for authorizing systems without losing sight of risk.
frameworks.summary: The RMF is NIST's life-cycle method for managing security and privacy risk across an enterprise. It connects system categorization, control selection, assessment, authorization and continuous monitoring into one governance loop.
keyPoints: Seven steps: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize and Monitor.
The Prepare step establishes roles, risk tolerance and the organization-wide view before system work starts.
An authorization package records the boundary, controls, assessment results and risk decision.
Authorizing officials accept risk; they do not simply approve paperwork.
Continuous monitoring keeps controls effective as systems, threats and missions change.
The RMF integrates with the SDLC, CSF 2.0 and enterprise risk management.
crownJewels: The authorization boundary and the system inventory inside it.
Security categorization and the rationale behind impact levels.
Authorization decisions, conditions and accepted risks.
Plans of action and milestones with owners and dates.
Monitoring evidence that proves controls still work.
clientUse: Structure an ATO or authorization programme around the seven steps.
Define system boundaries early to prevent sprawling assessment scope.
Use the package to brief authorizing officials on residual risk, not just compliance.
Build a continuous-monitoring calendar with meaningful metrics.

frameworks.title: NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3
frameworks.hook: The baseline for protecting controlled unclassified information in contractor systems.
frameworks.summary: SP 800-171 defines the security requirements for protecting controlled unclassified information (CUI) in non-federal systems. Revision 3 modernizes the text, aligns it with SP 800-53 and strengthens the link to CMMC assessments.
keyPoints: Requirements are organized into seventeen families covering access, audit, configuration, incident response and supply chain.
The standard applies to contractor systems that process, store or transmit CUI.
Tailoring allows requirements to be marked not applicable or satisfied by another control with justification.
SP 800-171A provides assessment procedures; SPRS records the contractor's self-assessment score.
Prime contractors flow the requirements down to subcontractors that touch CUI.
CMMC Level 2 uses the 800-171 requirements as its practice set.
crownJewels: CUI in documents, drawings, test data, maintenance records and communications.
Covered contractor information systems and their authorization boundaries.
Privileged accounts and remote-access paths into CUI environments.
Incident evidence and reporting channels to the DoD.
Subcontractor and supplier connections that extend the CUI footprint.
clientUse: Run a scoped gap assessment against Rev. 3 and document tailoring decisions.
Build the system security plan and POA&M that CMMC assessors will expect.
Calculate and validate the SPRS score before affirmation.
Map CUI flows to identify unnecessary data and reduce assessment scope.

frameworks.title: CMMC 2.0
frameworks.hook: The US defense supply chain's cyber certification and its assessment gates.
frameworks.summary: The Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification requires defense contractors to demonstrate implementation of specified security practices. CMMC 2.0 introduced three levels, streamlined assessments and a phased rollout tied to DoD contracts.
keyPoints: Level 1 (Foundational) covers 17 basic safeguarding practices and requires annual self-assessment.
Level 2 (Advanced) aligns with NIST SP 800-171 and requires third-party assessment for most contractors.
Level 3 (Expert) builds on SP 800-172 for the most critical programmes and uses government-led assessment.
Contractors must scope CUI and FCI, document practices and maintain evidence between assessments.
Affirmations and subcontractor flow-down extend accountability across the supply chain.
The final rule made CMMC a contract requirement, with implementation phased by acquisition.
crownJewels: Federal contract information and controlled unclassified information.
The CUI enclave and the systems that can reach it.
Assessment evidence, system security plans and POA&Ms.
Subcontractor relationships that handle CUI or FCI.
Identity, logging and incident response capabilities in scope.
clientUse: Determine the required CMMC level from the contract and data flow.
Scope the assessment boundary tightly before investing in remediation.
Prepare a C3PAO-ready evidence pack and close POA&M items.
Align CMMC, 800-171 and FedRAMP workstreams where they overlap.

frameworks.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022
frameworks.hook: The certifiable management system that turns security into a business process.
frameworks.summary: ISO/IEC 27001 specifies requirements for an information security management system (ISMS). It is risk-based, auditable and certifiable, and it anchors security governance in leadership, evidence and continual improvement.
keyPoints: Clauses 4 to 10 cover context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement.
Risk assessment and treatment must be repeatable and linked to a Statement of Applicability.
Annex A contains 93 controls grouped into organizational, people, physical and technological themes.
Certification requires an accredited audit, management review and evidence of operation over time.
The 2022 revision added threat intelligence, cloud, data leakage and secure coding controls.
The 2013 edition transition ended in 2025, making 2022 the current baseline.
crownJewels: The ISMS scope, risk register and Statement of Applicability.
Leadership decisions, resources and management-review evidence.
Operational records that prove controls work in practice.
Supplier, cloud and access-control evidence across the scope.
Internal audit findings, corrective actions and improvement history.
clientUse: Stand up a pragmatic ISMS rather than a documentation factory.
Use a gap analysis against Annex A to focus remediation and certification effort.
Build the Statement of Applicability with clear inclusion and exclusion rationales.
Run internal audits that sample evidence and challenge control ownership.

frameworks.title: ISO/IEC 27002:2022
frameworks.hook: The implementation playbook behind ISO 27001's Annex A.
frameworks.summary: ISO/IEC 27002 explains how to interpret and implement the 93 controls referenced by ISO 27001. It is guidance, not a certifiable management system, and helps teams move from control names to practical design choices.
keyPoints: Controls are grouped into organizational, people, physical and technological themes.
Each control has a purpose statement and implementation guidance, with related-control notes.
Attributes help filter controls by type, information property, cybersecurity concept and capability.
The 2022 edition consolidated and renamed many 2013 controls, so mappings matter during transition.
Guidance supports tailoring: not every control is relevant to every risk scenario.
It can be used with ISO 27001 or as a standalone control reference.
crownJewels: Control design decisions and the risks they address.
Named control owners and operating evidence.
Exceptions, compensating controls and residual risk.
Supplier and cloud control expectations.
Awareness, access and monitoring practices that support the controls.
clientUse: Turn Annex A controls into implementable standards with owners and evidence.
Use attributes to build a control library that maps cleanly to NIST and CIS.
Pressure-test whether controls are designed for the client's real threat model.
Support ISO 27001 audits with operating evidence, not just policy text.

frameworks.title: ISO/IEC 27005:2022
frameworks.hook: A repeatable method for turning threat and vulnerability data into risk decisions.
frameworks.summary: ISO/IEC 27005 provides guidance on managing information security risk in a way that supports ISO/IEC 27001. It covers context, assessment, treatment, acceptance, communication and monitoring, with both qualitative and quantitative options.
keyPoints: Establish risk context, criteria, scope and the relationship to enterprise risk management.
Identify assets, threats, vulnerabilities, existing controls and consequences.
Analyse likelihood and impact, then evaluate results against risk criteria.
Choose from modify, retain, avoid or share, with documented residual risk.
Communicate and consult with stakeholders, then monitor and review continuously.
The method is technology-neutral and can support cloud, OT and third-party scenarios.
crownJewels: Asset and process inventories with ownership and business value.
Threat intelligence and vulnerability data relevant to the scope.
Business-impact analysis and consequence modelling.
The risk register, treatment plans and accepted residual risks.
Evidence of monitoring and risk re-assessment.
clientUse: Build a repeatable risk process instead of a one-off spreadsheet.
Use scenario-based assessments to make risk comparisons meaningful.
Tie treatment plans to owners, budgets and deadlines.
Present residual risk and acceptance decisions to executive risk owners.

frameworks.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1
frameworks.hook: 18 prioritized safeguards that stop the majority of commodity attacks.
frameworks.summary: The CIS Critical Security Controls are a prioritized set of 18 cyber defense actions, with safeguards tailored to three implementation groups. They are highly prescriptive, mapping-friendly and useful for building a practical baseline quickly.
keyPoints: Eighteen controls cover inventory, data, identity, configuration, vulnerabilities, logging and recovery.
Implementation Group 1 is essential hygiene for small or low-risk organizations.
IG2 adds maturity for enterprises; IG3 addresses sensitive or high-threat environments.
Safeguards are specific and measurable, with mappings to NIST, ISO and PCI.
Version 8.1 updated guidance and kept the IG structure for prioritization.
The controls are a strong starting point when a client has no mature framework.
crownJewels: Hardware and software inventories, including unauthorized assets.
Sensitive data, data flows and data-at-rest protections.
Privileged accounts and administrative pathways.
Vulnerability, patch and configuration state of exposed systems.
Backups and logging needed to recover and investigate.
clientUse: Use IG1 as a minimum baseline for resource-constrained clients.
Build a prioritized 90-day roadmap from the 18 controls.
Map CIS safeguards to ISO 27001 or NIST outcomes to avoid duplicate work.
Measure safeguard coverage and show risk reduction to leadership.

frameworks.title: FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk)
frameworks.hook: Quantify cyber risk in money, not heat-map colours.
frameworks.summary: FAIR is a quantitative risk-analysis model that expresses cyber risk as probable frequency and probable magnitude of loss. It gives security leaders a defensible way to compare scenarios, set tolerances and justify controls in financial terms.
keyPoints: Risk is decomposed into loss event frequency and loss magnitude.
Loss event frequency depends on threat event frequency and vulnerability.
Loss magnitude includes productivity, response, replacement, fines and reputation effects.
Control strength reduces frequency or magnitude; it can be modelled explicitly.
Monte Carlo simulation expresses uncertainty as a range, not a single number.
FAIR complements frameworks such as CSF and ISO 27001 by adding economics.
crownJewels: Revenue-generating assets and services with measurable downtime costs.
Sensitive data whose loss creates regulatory and reputational exposure.
Key third-party dependencies and concentration risk.
Decision quality: assumptions, ranges and confidence levels.
clientUse: Quantify the top three risk scenarios for a board or insurer.
Compare the risk reduction of competing controls against their cost.
Set risk tolerance in financial terms and monitor against it.
Document assumptions so the model can be challenged and updated.

frameworks.title: AICPA SOC 2 / Trust Services Criteria
frameworks.hook: The assurance report clients ask for when trust is the product.
frameworks.summary: SOC 2 reports provide independent assurance over controls at a service organization, based on the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. Security is always in scope; availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy are optional.
keyPoints: The five trust services criteria are security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy.
Type 1 reports on control design at a point in time; Type 2 tests operating effectiveness over a period.
Scope, system description and control boundaries are as important as the controls themselves.
Evidence must cover the full period, including incidents, changes and exceptions.
Subservice organizations can use carve-out or inclusive methods.
SOC 2 is not a certification and does not replace ISO 27001, though they overlap heavily.
crownJewels: Customer data, credentials and service availability.
Logical access, change management and monitoring controls.
Vendor and subservice organization oversight.
Incident records, exceptions and management responses.
The system description and evidence trail behind the report.
clientUse: Run a readiness assessment before committing to an audit period.
Build an evidence calendar so controls are proven every month, not at year-end.
Use SOC 2 for SaaS trust and pair it with ISO 27001 where global clients ask.
Review vendor SOC 2 reports for scope, period, exceptions and CUECs.

frameworks.title: NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) 4.0
frameworks.hook: The UK's outcome-based test for operators of essential services.
frameworks.summary: The CAF is the NCSC's outcome-focused assessment framework for organizations that provide essential services. Version 4.0 organizes 41 contributing outcomes under 14 principles and four objectives, and is used by UK regulators to assess cyber resilience.
keyPoints: The four objectives are managing security risk, protecting against attack, detecting events and minimizing impact.
Fourteen principles and 41 contributing outcomes describe what good resilience looks like.
The framework is outcome-based, deliberately avoiding a tick-box control checklist.
Sector regulators use CAF profiles and self-assessments to target assurance activity.
Version 4.0 updated the framework in 2025 and introduced a core profile.
It complements NIS regulations in the UK and is relevant beyond regulated sectors.
crownJewels: Essential functions and the assets, people and suppliers they depend on.
Regulated service continuity and incident response capability.
OT, cloud and third-party dependencies that could disrupt outcomes.
Board accountability, assurance evidence and improvement plans.
clientUse: Run a CAF self-assessment against the 41 outcomes and rate evidence quality.
Use the core profile to prioritize essential-function resilience.
Translate gaps into regulator-ready improvement plans with owners.
Align CAF evidence with ISO 27001 and NIST CSF where possible.

frameworks.title: ANSSI Guide d'hygiène informatique
frameworks.hook: France's 42 pragmatic measures for a healthier information system.
frameworks.summary: ANSSI's hygiene guide distils essential cyber hygiene into 42 concrete measures for organizations of all sizes. It covers governance, awareness, authentication, patching, backups, network segmentation and crisis preparation with a distinctly operational tone.
keyPoints: Forty-two measures are grouped into practical themes from inventory to incident response.
Strong authentication, least privilege and separate admin accounts are treated as basics.
Patching, backups and restore testing are framed as resilience controls, not IT chores.
Network segmentation, filtering and secure Wi-Fi are expected even in small environments.
Awareness and a named crisis team are part of the baseline.
The guide is available in French and English and underpins many ANSSI publications.
crownJewels: Critical business systems and the data they hold.
Administrator accounts and privileged access paths.
Backups, restore capability and offline copies.
Network segmentation and internet-facing services.
Incident contacts, crisis procedures and evidence.
clientUse: Use the 42 measures as a pragmatic SME baseline or audit checklist.
Anchor recommendations in a recognizable French regulatory language.
Prioritize identity, patching and backups before buying more tooling.
Build a one-page remediation plan with owners and due dates.

frameworks.title: BSI IT-Grundschutz
frameworks.hook: Germany's modular method for building a defensible baseline from the ground up.
frameworks.summary: IT-Grundschutz is BSI's methodology for establishing a measurable security baseline across business processes and IT systems. Its modules and protection-needs analysis support both a standalone baseline and ISO 27001 certification on a Grundschutz basis.
keyPoints: A protection-needs assessment determines how much security each process and asset requires.
The IT-Grundschutz Compendium provides modules with must, should and can requirements.
Organizations can follow the basis, standard or core approach depending on ambition and risk.
ISO 27001 certification can be pursued on the basis of IT-Grundschutz.
Modules cover applications, infrastructure, ICS/OT, cloud and mobile use.
The method is detailed, prescriptive and well suited to German regulated markets.
crownJewels: Business processes and the information assets that support them.
Protection-needs classifications and derived requirements.
OT, ICS and cloud modules with operational dependencies.
Supplier and outsourcing relationships that affect the baseline.
Audit evidence and implementation status per module.
clientUse: Use protection-needs analysis to size controls proportionately.
Select modules that match the client's real technology estate.
Map Grundschutz modules to ISO 27001 Annex A for certification efficiency.
Give German stakeholders a familiar, auditable methodology.

frameworks.title: ACSC Essential Eight
frameworks.hook: Australia's eight mitigations that blunt ransomware and commodity intrusions.
frameworks.summary: The Essential Eight is a prioritized set of eight mitigation strategies designed to make commodity attacks significantly harder. Each strategy has maturity levels, allowing organizations to measure progress from ad hoc to resilient.
keyPoints: Application control and application patching close common malware paths.
Macro and user-application hardening reduce phishing payloads.
Restricting administrative privileges limits the blast radius of compromise.
Operating-system patching and multi-factor authentication protect the endpoint and identity layer.
Regular backups, tested restores and offline copies underpin recovery.
Maturity levels ML1 to ML3 describe increasing resistance to increasingly capable adversaries.
crownJewels: Endpoints, servers and the applications that execute on them.
Privileged accounts and administrative pathways.
Identity providers, MFA tokens and recovery processes.
Backups and the ability to restore critical services.
clientUse: Use the eight strategies as a ransomware-readiness baseline.
Assess maturity and build a sequenced improvement roadmap.
Prioritize application control, MFA and backups for the fastest risk reduction.
Report progress in a language familiar to Australian regulators and boards.

frameworks.title: CISA Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals
frameworks.hook: A minimum viable baseline of outcomes for critical infrastructure.
frameworks.summary: CISA's Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals define a common set of voluntary outcomes for critical infrastructure owners and operators. They prioritize foundational practices that reduce risk quickly and give under-resourced organizations a place to start.
keyPoints: Goals cover account security, device security, data security and governance.
Additional goals address vulnerability management, supply chain, incident response and recovery.
Sector-specific goals extend the common baseline for particular critical-infrastructure environments.
The goals are voluntary and intended to complement frameworks such as NIST CSF.
They help prioritize investments and communicate minimum expectations to leadership.
Mappings to other standards reduce duplicate assessment work.
crownJewels: Critical infrastructure services and operational technology.
Identity, device and data controls at the foundation of operations.
Backups, recovery capability and incident-response readiness.
Supply-chain visibility and third-party dependencies.
clientUse: Establish a minimum baseline for clients with limited cybersecurity maturity.
Use the goals to support grant applications and budget conversations.
Map existing NIST CSF work to CPGs to reduce duplicate reporting.
Focus first on the foundational goals that cut across sectors.

frameworks.title: NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture
frameworks.hook: Never trust the network; verify every request to every resource.
frameworks.summary: SP 800-207 defines zero trust architecture as a set of principles and logical components that remove implicit trust from the network. Access is granted per session based on identity, device posture, context and policy, with continuous monitoring.
keyPoints: Treat every data source and service as a resource, regardless of network location.
Secure all communication, internal or external, as if the network is hostile.
Grant access per session after dynamic policy evaluation; do not rely on static VPN trust.
Use a policy engine, policy administrator and policy enforcement points as the control plane.
Collect telemetry on identity, devices, traffic and behavior to improve decisions.
Micro-segmentation, software-defined perimeters and identity-aware proxies are key enablers.
Zero trust is an architecture journey, not a product category or a single purchase.
crownJewels: Crown-jewel applications and the data they expose.
Identities, device posture and the policy decision points.
Policy definitions, logs and continuous-monitoring telemetry.
Sensitive administrative interfaces and service accounts.
clientUse: Map the client's protect surface and prioritize the highest-value applications.
Define the policy engine and enforcement points before buying tools.
Sequence the journey around identity, device trust and micro-segmentation.
Measure reduced implicit trust and improved detection, not just tool deployment.

frameworks.title: ISO/IEC 27017:2015 Cloud Security Controls
frameworks.hook: Cloud-specific guidance for the shared-responsibility line.
frameworks.summary: ISO/IEC 27017 gives cloud service customers and providers guidance on applying ISO/IEC 27002 controls in cloud environments. It clarifies who is responsible for what and adds controls for cloud-specific risks such as virtual environments and administrative access.
keyPoints: Distinguishes the responsibilities of cloud service customers and cloud service providers.
Adds cloud-specific controls and implementation guidance to the 27002 baseline.
Addresses shared infrastructure, virtualization, tenant separation and administrative access.
Covers asset ownership, data deletion, logging and monitoring in cloud services.
Helps define contract expectations and provider assurance questions.
It is a control guidance standard, not a certification scheme by itself.
crownJewels: Tenant data and workloads hosted in shared infrastructure.
Cloud provider and customer administrative credentials.
The virtualization layer and management plane.
Data deletion, backup and portability evidence.
Shared logs and monitoring data that cross responsibility boundaries.
clientUse: Clarify shared-responsibility splits before signing a cloud contract.
Assess provider controls against customer-side obligations and gaps.
Use it to extend an ISO 27001 ISMS into cloud services.
Build a provider-assurance questionnaire around the cloud-specific controls.

frameworks.title: CSA Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) v4.1
frameworks.hook: A cloud control library that maps the alphabet soup for you.
frameworks.summary: The CSA Cloud Controls Matrix is a cloud-specific control framework with 197 control objectives across 17 domains. It maps controls to major standards, supports cloud assurance and underpins the CSA STAR programme.
keyPoints: 197 control objectives are organized into 17 security domains.
Controls cover governance, identity, data security, operations, resilience and third parties.
Cross-mappings reduce effort across ISO 27001, NIST, PCI DSS and other regimes.
The matrix supports both cloud service providers and cloud customers.
It is the control backbone of CSA STAR attestations and certifications.
Version 4.1 refines the v4 structure and keeps the cloud control language current.
crownJewels: Tenant data, identities and encryption keys.
Cloud management planes and APIs.
Logging, monitoring and incident evidence across shared infrastructure.
Supply-chain and sub-provider dependencies.
clientUse: Build a cloud control matrix and map it to the client's existing framework.
Assess providers consistently across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Use the mappings to avoid duplicated questionnaires and audits.
Anchor cloud assurance conversations around a shared vocabulary.

frameworks.title: FedRAMP
frameworks.hook: The gate for selling cloud services to the US federal government.
frameworks.summary: FedRAMP authorizes cloud service offerings for federal use against NIST SP 800-53 baselines. It combines independent assessment, government authorization and continuous monitoring, with a modernization effort aimed at faster, reusable assurance.
keyPoints: Baselines include LI-SaaS, Low, Moderate and High, built on NIST SP 800-53.
An independent 3PAO assesses the provider; a government authorizing official makes the risk decision.
Authorization packages include the SSP, assessment report, POA&M and continuous-monitoring plan.
Agency authorizations and the FedRAMP marketplace support reuse across government.
Continuous monitoring requires monthly or annual evidence and timely incident reporting.
FedRAMP 20x is reshaping the programme around automation and continuous assurance.
crownJewels: Federal data and the systems that process it.
The authorization boundary, including inherited controls and dependencies.
Assessment evidence, POA&Ms and continuous-monitoring data.
Supply-chain provenance and personnel screening.
clientUse: Determine the correct impact baseline before scoping the assessment.
Build a control inheritance model with the cloud infrastructure provider.
Prepare evidence and automation for continuous monitoring from day one.
Use the marketplace and reuse patterns for faster agency authorization.

frameworks.title: BSI Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue (C5)
frameworks.hook: Germany's rigorous cloud audit standard, trusted across Europe.
frameworks.summary: BSI C5 is a cloud-specific audit catalogue covering security, transparency and assurance. It is widely used by German and European customers to evaluate cloud providers, and can be attested by an independent auditor.
keyPoints: Covers governance, identity and access, encryption, operations, logging, procurement and compliance.
Requires transparency about the provider's security organization and control environment.
Independent auditors issue C5 attestation reports against the catalogue.
Addresses multi-tenancy, data location, portability and secure deletion.
Maps well to ISO 27001 but goes deeper on cloud-specific operational controls.
Version 2020 remains the reference; watch for newer BSI cloud guidance.
crownJewels: Customer data, metadata and encryption keys.
Multi-tenant isolation and administrative access.
Data location, deletion and portability controls.
Provider personnel, sub-processors and incident response.
clientUse: Use C5 attestations as a rigorous alternative to generic cloud questionnaires.
Map provider evidence to ISO 27001 and GDPR obligations.
Challenge scope, audit period and exceptions in the attestation.
Address data location and sub-processor risk for German clients.

frameworks.title: ANSSI SecNumCloud
frameworks.hook: France's sovereignty-focused qualification for trusted cloud providers.
frameworks.summary: SecNumCloud is ANSSI's qualification scheme for cloud service providers that meet demanding security and sovereignty requirements. It is particularly relevant for French public-sector and critical-infrastructure customers handling sensitive data.
keyPoints: Covers governance, access control, encryption, resilience and supply-chain security.
Adds sovereignty criteria around control by non-EU actors and exposure to foreign law.
Qualification requires an audit and ongoing surveillance by ANSSI-accredited assessors.
Distinguishes different service models and deployment scopes.
Commonly requested for sensitive French public-sector and OIV work.
It is a qualification, not a generic ISO-style certification.
crownJewels: Sensitive and sovereign data hosted in the cloud.
Provider ownership, control and exposure to non-EU jurisdiction.
Encryption, key management and administrative access.
Supply-chain dependencies and provider exit capability.
clientUse: Assess sovereignty requirements before choosing a cloud provider.
Verify qualification scope and the services actually covered.
Use the referential to challenge provider control and sub-processor claims.
Plan an exit strategy that preserves data portability and service continuity.

frameworks.title: CIS Benchmarks
frameworks.hook: Prescriptive hardening settings for the platforms you actually run.
frameworks.summary: CIS Benchmarks are consensus-developed hardening guides for cloud platforms, operating systems, databases, browsers and network devices. Each benchmark provides auditable settings at Level 1 and Level 2, with automated assessment options.
keyPoints: Benchmarks exist for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Windows, Linux, databases and network devices.
Level 1 is basic hygiene; Level 2 adds defense in depth for higher-risk environments.
Recommendations are specific, testable and mapped to CIS Controls.
CIS-CAT and third-party tools automate configuration assessment.
Organizations must tailor settings to operational requirements and document exceptions.
Drift is the enemy: benchmark once, then continuously verify.
crownJewels: Root and administrative accounts on every platform.
Logging, monitoring and audit trails.
Network exposure, identity configuration and encryption settings.
Operating-system and application hardening state.
Configuration drift and exception records.
clientUse: Select benchmarks for the actual platform estate, not the entire catalogue.
Use Level 1 for a defensible baseline; justify Level 2 deviations.
Automate assessment and feed drift into vulnerability management.
Document exceptions with owners, risk rationale and expiry dates.

frameworks.title: OWASP Kubernetes Top 10
frameworks.hook: The cluster misconfigurations attackers look for first.
frameworks.summary: The OWASP Kubernetes Top 10 catalogues the most common security risks in Kubernetes environments. It focuses on misconfiguration, identity, supply chain and visibility gaps that turn a cluster into an attack path.
keyPoints: Insecure workload configurations expose secrets, host paths and privileged containers.
Supply-chain vulnerabilities enter through images, charts and third-party components.
Over-permissive RBAC and service accounts create lateral movement paths.
Missing network policies and segmentation allow unrestricted pod-to-pod traffic.
Secrets management, control-plane exposure and inadequate logging are recurring failures.
Admission control, policy-as-code and image signing are core mitigations.
crownJewels: Cluster control plane, API server and etcd.
Service accounts, tokens and workload identity.
Container images, registries and build pipelines.
Secrets, persistent volumes and tenant workloads.
Audit logs and runtime telemetry.
clientUse: Assess the cluster against the Top 10 before migrating production workloads.
Prioritize RBAC, network policy and admission control as structural fixes.
Integrate image scanning and signing into the build pipeline.
Use runtime detection to catch what configuration reviews miss.

frameworks.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
frameworks.hook: A shared risk language for AI that boards and builders can both use.
frameworks.summary: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides a voluntary, use-case-neutral approach to managing risks from AI systems. Its four functions - Govern, Map, Measure and Manage - support trustworthy AI across the lifecycle.
keyPoints: Govern creates accountability, policies, roles and a risk culture around AI.
Map establishes context, affected stakeholders and the specific risks of each AI use case.
Measure analyses, benchmarks and monitors risk and trustworthiness characteristics.
Manage prioritizes, treats and monitors risks, including residual risk and incidents.
Trustworthiness covers validity, safety, security, accountability, transparency, privacy and fairness.
Profiles adapt the framework to sectors, technologies or specific use cases.
It is voluntary but widely used as the reference structure for AI governance.
crownJewels: AI models, weights, prompts and system instructions.
Training, fine-tuning and retrieval data, including personal information.
Agent tools, connectors and credentials that can act on the real world.
Affected people and the decisions or services the AI influences.
clientUse: Inventory AI use cases and classify them by risk before buying controls.
Use Govern to assign an accountable owner and a clear risk appetite.
Build a measurement plan that includes security, privacy and fairness testing.
Turn the framework into an AI governance operating model, not a one-off assessment.

frameworks.title: NIST Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1)
frameworks.hook: The AI RMF, sharpened for generative models and their unique failure modes.
frameworks.summary: NIST AI 600-1 is a cross-sector profile that applies the AI RMF to generative AI. It identifies risks that are amplified or novel in GenAI and suggests actions for developers, deployers and users across the lifecycle.
keyPoints: Covers risks such as confabulation, data privacy, harmful bias, information integrity and security.
Highlights prompt injection, data leakage and supply-chain risk in model ecosystems.
Provides suggested actions mapped to the AI RMF functions and lifecycle stages.
Emphasizes testing, evaluation, red teaming and human oversight before deployment.
Addresses provenance, transparency and content authentication for generated media.
Useful as a checklist when a client is deploying an LLM or copilot.
crownJewels: System prompts, retrieval corpora and conversation data.
Model weights, adapters and fine-tuning datasets.
Tool access, plugins and agent credentials.
Generated content that influences decisions or public trust.
clientUse: Run a GenAI-specific risk assessment before piloting a copilot or agent.
Add prompt-injection and data-leakage tests to the security test plan.
Define human-review triggers for high-impact outputs.
Document model provenance and content-authenticity measures.

frameworks.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI Management System
frameworks.hook: The certifiable management system for responsible AI.
frameworks.summary: ISO/IEC 42001 specifies requirements for an artificial intelligence management system (AIMS). It gives organizations a certifiable, risk-based structure for AI governance, lifecycle controls and continual improvement.
keyPoints: Uses the same Annex SL management-system structure as ISO 27001 and ISO 22301.
Requires an AI policy, roles, risk assessment and a statement of applicability.
Annex A controls address AI impact assessment, data, model lifecycle, third parties and transparency.
Emphasizes human oversight and accountability for AI-enabled decisions.
Integrates with information security, privacy and quality management systems.
Certification is possible through accredited bodies, though the standard is still new.
crownJewels: AI system inventory and the business processes they affect.
Training and operational data, including personal information.
Model artifacts, prompts and evaluation evidence.
Human-oversight records and impact assessments.
Third-party models, APIs and data suppliers.
clientUse: Use it to build an AI management system that can be audited.
Combine it with ISO 27001 to avoid parallel governance structures.
Require AI impact assessments for high-consequence use cases.
Map supplier obligations and evidence into the AIMS.

frameworks.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
frameworks.hook: The ten ways LLM applications get exploited in production.
frameworks.summary: The OWASP LLM Top 10 catalogues the most critical security risks for applications built on large language models. It is a practical checklist for threat modelling, testing and securing copilots, RAG systems and AI agents.
keyPoints: Prompt injection can override instructions or hijack tool use, including indirect injection through documents.
Sensitive information disclosure exposes prompts, training data, secrets or other users' data.
Supply-chain risks enter through models, datasets, plugins and dependencies.
Data and model poisoning can corrupt behavior and outputs.
Improper output handling turns model text into XSS, command execution or unsafe downstream actions.
Excessive agency gives the model tools and permissions beyond what the task requires.
System prompt leakage, vector-store weaknesses, misinformation and unbounded consumption round out the list.
crownJewels: System prompts and hidden instructions.
Retrieval corpora, embeddings and vector databases.
Tool credentials, APIs and agent memory.
Model weights, fine-tuning data and user conversations.
clientUse: Threat-model every LLM feature with the Top 10 as a prompt sheet.
Test indirect prompt injection through email, documents and web content.
Apply least privilege to tools and require confirmation for high-impact actions.
Add output encoding and validation before model text reaches other systems.

frameworks.title: MITRE ATLAS
frameworks.hook: ATT&CK for AI: the tactics and techniques used against machine learning.
frameworks.summary: MITRE ATLAS is a knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and case studies targeting AI and machine learning systems. It helps security teams map threats, design detections and test defenses across the ML lifecycle.
keyPoints: Organizes adversarial behavior across reconnaissance, access, staging, exfiltration and impact.
Includes techniques specific to ML, such as data poisoning, model evasion and prompt injection.
Case studies connect techniques to real-world incidents and research.
Mappings to ATT&CK help integrate AI threats into existing detection programmes.
Supports threat modelling, red teaming and control validation.
The knowledge base evolves with new AI attack research.
crownJewels: Training and fine-tuning datasets.
Model weights, architecture and intellectual property.
Inference APIs, prompts and user data.
ML pipelines, feature stores and deployment infrastructure.
Agent tools and downstream systems the model can influence.
clientUse: Use ATLAS to threat-model an AI system end to end.
Map AI techniques to existing ATT&CK detections where they overlap.
Design red-team exercises around realistic AI attack paths.
Prioritize controls by the techniques most relevant to the use case.

frameworks.title: ANSSI Security Recommendations for Generative AI
frameworks.hook: France's architecture-first playbook for deploying generative AI safely.
frameworks.summary: ANSSI's generative AI guide sets out security recommendations for designing, deploying and operating a GenAI system. It focuses on architecture, data protection, access control, output validation and human oversight.
keyPoints: Define the use case, threat model and trust boundaries before choosing a model.
Isolate the AI system from sensitive information systems and apply least privilege to connectors.
Protect prompts, models and data with encryption, access control and logging.
Validate and control outputs before they trigger actions or reach users.
Keep humans accountable for high-impact decisions and provide a way to contest outputs.
Monitor usage, detect anomalies and prepare an incident response plan for AI-specific failures.
ANSSI and BSI have also published joint zero-trust design principles for LLM systems.
crownJewels: Sensitive data and prompts sent to the model.
Model weights, adapters and system instructions.
Connectors, plugins and credentials the model can use.
Outputs that feed business decisions or other systems.
Usage logs and personal data processed by the service.
clientUse: Use it to review a GenAI architecture before production.
Draw trust boundaries between the model, data sources and business systems.
Add output validation and human approval for consequential actions.
Align AI security with French and EU regulatory expectations.

frameworks.title: EU Artificial Intelligence Act
frameworks.hook: The risk-based law that is reshaping AI product design worldwide.
frameworks.summary: The EU AI Act establishes a risk-based legal framework for AI systems placed on the EU market. It prohibits certain practices, imposes transparency duties, and places extensive obligations on high-risk AI and general-purpose AI models.
keyPoints: Unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited, including certain social scoring and manipulation uses.
High-risk systems must meet requirements for risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight and cybersecurity.
Limited-risk systems have transparency obligations, such as disclosing AI interaction or synthetic content.
General-purpose AI models face documentation, copyright and systemic-risk obligations.
Providers must operate a quality management system, conduct conformity assessment and apply CE marking.
Post-market monitoring, incident reporting and technical documentation are ongoing duties.
Implementation is phased, so scope and timing must be checked for each use case.
crownJewels: High-risk AI systems and the decisions they influence.
Training, validation and testing datasets.
Technical documentation, logs and conformity evidence.
Human-oversight design and incident records.
General-purpose model capabilities and systemic-risk evaluations.
clientUse: Classify each AI use case against the Act's risk tiers.
Build a technical file and quality-management system for high-risk systems.
Check supply-chain roles: provider, deployer, importer and distributor.
Connect AI Act evidence to ISO 42001 and NIST AI RMF work.

frameworks.title: OWASP Top 10:2025
frameworks.hook: The baseline language for web application risk.
frameworks.summary: The OWASP Top 10 is the most widely used awareness document for web application security. The 2025 edition adds software supply chain failures and mishandling of exceptional conditions to the long-standing access-control and injection risks.
keyPoints: A01 Broken Access Control remains the top risk in web applications.
A02 Security Misconfiguration covers cloud defaults, verbose errors and unnecessary features.
A03 Software Supply Chain Failures is new and elevates dependency and build-system risk.
A04 Cryptographic Failures and A05 Injection remain core engineering concerns.
A06 Insecure Design and A07 Authentication Failures address architecture and identity.
A08 Integrity Failures, A09 Logging and Alerting Failures and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions close the list.
The Top 10 is an awareness baseline, not a complete verification standard.
crownJewels: Authentication and session state.
Access-control decisions and object-level authorization.
Source code, dependencies and build pipelines.
Secrets, keys and sensitive configuration.
Logs and alerting that reveal or miss attacks.
clientUse: Use it to frame developer awareness and secure-coding training.
Map findings from penetration tests and scanners to the categories.
Pair it with ASVS when you need verifiable requirements.
Prioritize access control, supply chain and authentication for 2025 programmes.

frameworks.title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) 5.0
frameworks.hook: Testable application security requirements, not just good advice.
frameworks.summary: ASVS 5.0 defines verifiable security requirements for applications and their APIs. It lets teams specify assurance levels, scope assessments consistently and turn application security into evidence-based verification.
keyPoints: Three verification levels support different assurance needs, from baseline to high-assurance applications.
Requirements span architecture, authentication, session management, access control and input validation.
Cryptography, data protection, communications, configuration and file handling are covered in depth.
API and web requirements are integrated rather than treated as separate worlds.
Each requirement can be tested and evidenced, making it suitable for procurement and audits.
Version 5.0 restructured the standard and clarified requirements for modern applications.
crownJewels: Authentication, session and access-control logic.
Sensitive data, cryptographic keys and secrets.
API endpoints and business logic that enforce authorization.
Input handling, file upload and output encoding paths.
Security logging and error handling evidence.
clientUse: Pick a verification level based on data sensitivity and exposure.
Use ASVS as acceptance criteria in development and procurement contracts.
Scope penetration tests and code reviews with explicit ASVS chapters.
Track requirement-level evidence instead of a single pass/fail report.

frameworks.title: OWASP API Security Top 10:2023
frameworks.hook: The authorization failures that dominate API breaches.
frameworks.summary: The OWASP API Security Top 10 focuses on the risks that are specific to APIs, especially broken object-level authorization and business-flow abuse. It is essential for any organization exposing internal or partner APIs.
keyPoints: API1 Broken Object Level Authorization lets users access objects belonging to others.
API2 Broken Authentication covers weak token and credential handling.
API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization exposes or mass-assigns sensitive fields.
API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption enables abuse through expensive or unbounded calls.
API5 Broken Function Level Authorization and API6 sensitive business flows enable privilege and fraud abuse.
API7 SSRF, API8 misconfiguration, API9 inventory gaps and API10 unsafe third-party consumption complete the list.
Traditional web scanners often miss these problems; test the business logic.
crownJewels: Object identifiers and tenant boundaries.
Tokens, API keys and authentication flows.
Sensitive object properties and admin functions.
Business flows such as payments, referrals and password resets.
The API inventory, versions and deprecated endpoints.
clientUse: Test every object and function for authorization, not just authentication.
Inventory all APIs, including shadow and deprecated versions.
Set rate limits, quotas and cost controls for expensive operations.
Review third-party API consumption and trust assumptions.

frameworks.title: OWASP Software Assurance Maturity Model (SAMM) 2.0
frameworks.hook: Measure and improve how your organization builds secure software.
frameworks.summary: SAMM is a maturity model for software assurance across the development lifecycle. It organizes 15 security practices into five business functions, with incremental maturity levels and assessment guidance.
keyPoints: Five business functions: Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification and Operations.
Fifteen practices cover strategy, policy, education, threat assessment, secure architecture and testing.
Maturity levels 0 to 3 describe increasingly institutionalized practices.
Assessment worksheets help gather evidence and score each practice.
The model is technology-agnostic and scales from small teams to enterprises.
It pairs well with SSDF and ASVS for a complete AppSec programme.
crownJewels: Software development lifecycle and release process.
Source code, dependencies and build artifacts.
Security requirements, threat models and test evidence.
Developer training and security champions.
Production monitoring and vulnerability response.
clientUse: Run a SAMM assessment to baseline AppSec maturity.
Build a multi-quarter roadmap focused on a few practices at a time.
Use maturity scores to show progress to engineering leadership.
Connect SAMM improvements to SSDF and ASVS requirements.

frameworks.title: NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
frameworks.hook: A common baseline for secure software development and supplier assurance.
frameworks.summary: The SSDF defines a set of secure software development practices that organizations can integrate into their SDLC. It is used for internal programmes and for supplier attestations, including US federal software acquisition.
keyPoints: Four practice groups: Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software and Respond to Vulnerabilities.
Prepare the Organization establishes policy, roles, tooling and training.
Protect the Software secures the development environment, code and build pipeline.
Produce Well-Secured Software covers secure design, coding, testing and release.
Respond to Vulnerabilities covers intake, analysis, remediation and disclosure.
SP 800-218A extends the framework to generative AI and dual-use foundation models.
The framework is outcome-based and maps to common SDLC practices.
crownJewels: Source code, secrets and intellectual property.
Build systems, CI/CD pipelines and signing keys.
Third-party components and their provenance.
Vulnerability reports and disclosure channels.
Release artifacts and update mechanisms.
clientUse: Build a secure SDLC roadmap around the four practice groups.
Use SSDF attestations as supplier evidence for federal and enterprise buyers.
Secure the build pipeline, not just the code review process.
Extend the practices to AI model development with SP 800-218A.

frameworks.title: CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses
frameworks.hook: The coding mistakes most likely to become real vulnerabilities.
frameworks.summary: The CWE Top 25 is MITRE's ranked list of the most dangerous software weaknesses, based on real vulnerability data. It helps development teams prioritize secure-coding standards, code review and static-analysis rules.
keyPoints: Ranks weaknesses by prevalence and severity in real-world vulnerability data.
Covers injection, memory safety, access control, authentication, path traversal and deserialization.
Maps to CWE identifiers that tools and secure-coding standards can reference.
Useful for tuning SAST rules and developer training.
The list changes annually, so policies should be reviewed.
It complements OWASP Top 10 and ASVS with a weakness-level view.
crownJewels: Source code and input-handling logic.
Memory-unsafe components and native libraries.
Authentication and authorization checks.
Deserialization and file-processing paths.
Secure-coding standards and tool coverage.
clientUse: Tune SAST and code-review checklists to the Top 25.
Build developer training around the weaknesses found in actual code.
Prioritize memory-safety work in native and embedded code.
Track whether top weaknesses recur across releases.

frameworks.title: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts)
frameworks.hook: Prove how your software was built, not just what it contains.
frameworks.summary: SLSA is a framework for improving software supply-chain integrity through build provenance, source integrity and hardened build platforms. Its levels give buyers and builders a shared way to describe assurance.
keyPoints: Focuses on source integrity, build integrity and artifact provenance.
Build levels progress from documented builds to hardened, isolated, reproducible build platforms.
Provenance attestations record what was built, from which source and by which builder.
Signed provenance helps consumers verify an artifact before deployment.
SLSA complements SBOMs: SBOMs describe components, SLSA describes how the artifact was produced.
Adoption can be incremental along a build or source track.
crownJewels: Source repositories and commit history.
Build systems, CI runners and release pipelines.
Signing keys and attestation trust roots.
Release artifacts and distribution channels.
Dependencies and third-party builders.
clientUse: Assess the client's build pipeline against the SLSA levels.
Require provenance for critical software and verify it at deployment.
Harden CI identity, isolation and secret handling first.
Use SLSA alongside SBOM and SSDF for a complete supply-chain story.

frameworks.title: CISA Secure by Design
frameworks.hook: Shift the burden of security from customers to product makers.
frameworks.summary: Secure by Design is CISA's call for technology manufacturers to build security into products by default. It defines three principles and a set of tactics for making secure outcomes the default, not an optional add-on.
keyPoints: Take ownership of customer security outcomes rather than shifting the burden.
Embrace radical transparency and accountability, including vulnerability disclosure.
Lead from the top so product security is a business priority.
Secure-by-default tactics include MFA, no default passwords and safe configuration.
Memory-safe languages and secure update mechanisms reduce whole classes of defects.
The guidance is relevant to software, hardware, IoT and cloud services.
crownJewels: Customer data and the products that process it.
Default credentials and initial configuration.
Update and vulnerability-disclosure channels.
Third-party components in the product.
Logging and incident transparency.
clientUse: Use the principles in product design reviews and vendor selection.
Ask suppliers for secure-by-default evidence, not just a security questionnaire.
Prioritize removal of default passwords and forced MFA.
Include vulnerability disclosure and update policy in contracts.

frameworks.title: NIST Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication (SP 800-63B-4)
frameworks.hook: The reference standard for modern, usable authentication.
frameworks.summary: SP 800-63B-4 defines authentication and authenticator-management requirements at three assurance levels. It modernizes password guidance, recognizes syncable authenticators and pushes organizations toward phishing-resistant authentication.
keyPoints: AAL1, AAL2 and AAL3 describe increasing confidence that a claimant controls an authenticator.
Passwords used alone must be at least 15 characters; passwords used with MFA must be at least 8.
No composition rules, no forced periodic rotation and no knowledge-based recovery questions.
Screen new passwords against blocklists and rate-limit authentication attempts.
Phishing-resistant authenticators are required at the highest assurance levels.
Syncable authenticators are recognized at AAL2, with requirements for recovery and device security.
Enrollment, reauthentication and authenticator lifecycle events must be managed explicitly.
crownJewels: Credentials, authenticators and recovery channels.
Identity-proofing data and enrollment records.
Session tokens and authentication logs.
Account recovery paths, which are often weaker than the login itself.
clientUse: Modernize password policy to length, blocklists and rate limiting.
Prioritize phishing-resistant MFA for administrators and high-value users.
Assess whether the authenticator mix meets the required AAL.
Design account recovery as a security-critical flow, not a helpdesk afterthought.

frameworks.title: FIDO2 / WebAuthn
frameworks.hook: Phishing-resistant sign-in built on public-key cryptography and passkeys.
frameworks.summary: FIDO2 combines the W3C WebAuthn API with the CTAP2 protocol to enable public-key authentication in browsers and apps. It underpins passkeys and is the leading path to phishing-resistant, passwordless authentication.
keyPoints: The authenticator holds a private key; the relying party stores only the public key.
Credentials are bound to the relying-party origin, which defeats classic phishing.
Passkeys can be device-bound or synced through a platform ecosystem.
Attestation can prove authenticator properties, but privacy and policy trade-offs matter.
Account recovery and device enrollment remain the weakest links in a passkey rollout.
FIDO2 works with platform biometrics, security keys and cross-device authentication.
crownJewels: Authenticator private keys and secure hardware.
Biometric templates and local device authentication.
Account recovery and device-enrollment channels.
Relying-party configuration, origins and attestation policy.
Session tokens issued after authentication.
clientUse: Make phishing-resistant MFA the default for administrators and high-risk users.
Design recovery before rollout; it is the most abused bypass.
Decide whether passkeys are syncable, device-bound or both by risk tier.
Test cross-device and platform-specific user journeys.

frameworks.title: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700)
frameworks.hook: The guardrails that stop OAuth deployments from becoming token leaks.
frameworks.summary: RFC 9700 consolidates the security best practices for OAuth 2.0 deployments. It addresses redirects, PKCE, token handling, sender-constrained tokens and the removal of insecure grant patterns.
keyPoints: Use authorization code flow with PKCE; avoid implicit and resource-owner password grants.
Redirect URIs must be exact and protected; open redirects are a classic token-theft path.
Sender-constrained tokens using DPoP or mutual TLS reduce bearer-token replay.
Access tokens should be audience-restricted and short-lived.
Refresh tokens need rotation, binding and revocation on compromise.
Client authentication, scope minimization and consent integrity are essential.
Token leakage can happen through logs, referrers, browsers and misconfigured apps.
crownJewels: Access and refresh tokens.
Client secrets and private keys.
Authorization codes and redirect URI configuration.
Consent grants and scopes with access to sensitive APIs.
Token logs and monitoring data.
clientUse: Review every OAuth client for PKCE, redirect URI and grant-type hygiene.
Prefer DPoP or mTLS for high-value APIs.
Set short token lifetimes and monitor anomalous token use.
Test consent screens for scope creep and redirect manipulation.

frameworks.title: NIST SP 800-153: Securing Wireless Local Area Networks
frameworks.hook: The enterprise WLAN baseline: policy, architecture, monitoring.
frameworks.summary: SP 800-153 provides guidelines for securing wireless local area networks in enterprises. It covers WLAN policy, architecture, authentication, segmentation, rogue access-point detection and ongoing monitoring, with WPA2-Enterprise as its technical reference point.
keyPoints: Establish a WLAN security policy and assign clear ownership before deploying technology.
Use enterprise authentication and strong encryption; treat open or shared-key networks as untrusted.
Separate guest, corporate and IoT wireless traffic with VLANs and firewall policy.
Detect and locate rogue access points and unauthorized ad hoc networks.
Harden access points, controllers and management interfaces.
Monitor the wireless spectrum and review logs continuously.
Pair the guide with current WPA3 and zero-trust guidance for new deployments.
crownJewels: Wireless credentials, certificates and RADIUS infrastructure.
Access points, controllers and their management planes.
Corporate and guest traffic on shared wireless infrastructure.
Rogue-device and wireless-monitoring evidence.
clientUse: Audit WLAN policy, segmentation and authentication against the guide.
Hunt for rogue access points and unauthorized wireless bridges.
Separate guest, OT and corporate traffic with enforceable policy.
Use it as a foundation, then upgrade design requirements to WPA3.

frameworks.title: Wi-Fi CERTIFIED WPA3
frameworks.hook: The current Wi-Fi security baseline, with forward secrecy and better handshakes.
frameworks.summary: WPA3 is the Wi-Fi Alliance's security certification for modern wireless networks. It replaces the WPA2 pre-shared-key handshake with SAE, adds 192-bit enterprise cryptography and protects open networks through OWE.
keyPoints: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) provides forward secrecy and resists offline dictionary attacks.
WPA3-Enterprise offers a 192-bit security mode for high-assurance environments.
OWE (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption) encrypts traffic on open guest networks.
Protected Management Frames defend against deauthentication and disassociation attacks.
WPA3 transition mode supports mixed WPA2/WPA3 estates but weakens the security story.
Device provisioning and IoT onboarding need separate design attention.
WPA3 does not fix weak passphrases, rogue APs or poor network segmentation.
crownJewels: Wi-Fi passphrases, PSKs and enterprise credentials.
RADIUS and identity infrastructure.
Access-point and controller management interfaces.
Guest, IoT and OT traffic that shares the wireless estate.
Wireless management frames and client associations.
clientUse: Set WPA3 as the target for new deployments and high-risk sites.
Use WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit for sensitive environments where supported.
Plan retirement of WPA2 transition mode and legacy IoT exceptions.
Pair WPA3 with segmentation, monitoring and certificate-based identity.

frameworks.title: NIST SP 800-121: Guide to Bluetooth Security
frameworks.hook: Security guidance for the personal-area network hiding in every pocket.
frameworks.summary: SP 800-121 explains how to secure Bluetooth and Bluetooth Low Energy deployments. It covers pairing models, link-layer security, device management and the risks created by discoverable devices and weak pairing.
keyPoints: Pairing mode determines whether the link is protected against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks.
Numeric comparison and passkey entry provide stronger protection than just-works pairing.
LE Secure Connections improve key exchange for Bluetooth Low Energy.
Disable unnecessary discoverability, pairing and profiles.
Use device management, allowlists and monitoring for enterprise Bluetooth fleets.
Assess Bluetooth keyboards, medical devices, wearables and industrial sensors by use case.
Check current Bluetooth SIG guidance alongside this older NIST baseline.
crownJewels: Bluetooth link keys, bonding data and device identities.
Input devices and peripherals that can inject keystrokes.
Wearables, medical devices and OT sensors carrying sensitive data.
Discoverable devices and unmanaged Bluetooth bridges.
clientUse: Inventory Bluetooth use and pair only approved device classes.
Ban just-works pairing for sensitive peripherals where possible.
Disable discoverability and unused profiles on managed devices.
Review medical, wearable and OT Bluetooth separately.

frameworks.title: Zigbee 3.0 Security
frameworks.hook: The trust-center model behind smart buildings, sensors and home automation.
frameworks.summary: Zigbee 3.0 unifies the application layer for low-power mesh networks and defines security through trust centers, network keys and install codes. It is common in building automation, smart meters, lighting and IoT sensor estates.
keyPoints: A trust center manages network security and distributes keys to joining devices.
Centralized security uses a single network key; distributed security gives some devices their own link keys.
Install codes reduce the risk of joining devices being accepted by the wrong network.
Over-the-air firmware updates must be signed and authenticated.
Weak key handling, default install codes and poor trust-center protection are common failures.
Network keys are shared secrets: one compromised device can expose the mesh.
crownJewels: The trust center and its master keys.
Network keys and device link keys.
Install codes and commissioning credentials.
Sensors, actuators and building-automation commands.
OTA firmware images and update signing keys.
clientUse: Review commissioning and trust-center design before deploying at scale.
Rotate default install codes and protect the trust center like a CA.
Verify firmware-signing and update processes.
Segment Zigbee networks from corporate and safety-critical OT networks.

frameworks.title: 3GPP 5G Security Architecture (TS 33.501)
frameworks.hook: The security architecture behind private 5G, network slicing and roaming.
frameworks.summary: TS 33.501 defines the 5G security architecture, including subscriber authentication, identity privacy, network-domain security, slicing and service-based interfaces. It is essential for telecom, private-5G and critical-network assessments.
keyPoints: 5G-AKA authenticates subscribers and establishes keys between the device and the network.
SUCI concealment protects the subscriber identity on the radio interface.
Service-based architecture secures signaling between network functions with TLS and OAuth-based service authorization.
Network slicing introduces new isolation and cross-slice security requirements.
Roaming uses the SEPP to protect inter-operator signaling.
Private 5G and edge deployments add cloud and OT risks beyond the 3GPP scope.
The standard evolves with each 3GPP release; always check the applicable release.
crownJewels: Subscriber credentials, SIM/eSIM data and authentication keys.
Signaling between network functions and roaming partners.
Network slices and the isolation between tenants.
Management, orchestration and edge infrastructure.
User-plane traffic and metadata.
clientUse: Scope private-5G assessments by release, architecture and slice design.
Review subscriber identity privacy, roaming and interconnect security.
Assess slice isolation alongside cloud and OT controls.
Include the management plane and supply chain, not just the radio.

frameworks.title: NFC and EMV Contactless Security
frameworks.hook: How tap-to-pay protects the PAN, and where relay and skimming risks remain.
frameworks.summary: NFC and EMV contactless standards govern tap-to-pay, mobile wallets and tokenized card credentials. Security relies on short-range communication, dynamic cryptograms, secure elements and network-level tokenization, not on the PAN alone.
keyPoints: EMV contactless transactions use dynamic cryptograms that change per transaction.
Tokenization replaces the PAN with a payment token restricted to a device or domain.
Secure elements and trusted execution environments protect mobile-wallet keys.
Relay attacks extend range and can bypass the physical proximity assumption.
Cardholder verification methods and transaction risk rules affect fraud exposure.
Merchant terminals and payment apps must protect keys, firmware and card data.
NFC is also used for access badges and identity documents, with different threat models.
crownJewels: Primary account numbers and payment tokens.
EMV keys, cryptograms and secure-element credentials.
POS terminals and payment-app firmware.
Cardholder verification data and transaction logs.
Access-badge and identity credentials carried over NFC.
clientUse: Assess tokenization and secure-element use, not just PCI scope.
Test for relay and skimming scenarios in payment journeys.
Review terminal firmware, key management and tamper evidence.
Separate payment NFC from physical-access credentials.

frameworks.title: EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
frameworks.hook: The privacy law that made data protection a board-level risk.
frameworks.summary: The GDPR governs the processing of personal data in the EU and EEA and applies extraterritorially to many organizations outside Europe. It combines principles, lawful bases, data-subject rights, accountability, breach notification and transfer rules with significant fines.
keyPoints: Seven principles: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; accountability.
Every processing activity needs a lawful basis and, for special categories, an additional condition.
Data-subject rights include access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and objection.
Controllers must maintain records, run DPIAs for high-risk processing and appoint a DPO where required.
Personal-data breaches must be notified to the supervisory authority within 72 hours where required.
International transfers need an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards such as SCCs plus a transfer assessment.
Fines can reach EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.
crownJewels: Personal data, especially special-category data and data on vulnerable people.
Records of processing, lawful-basis decisions and DPIAs.
Data-subject request evidence and consent records.
Processor agreements and international-transfer safeguards.
Breach records, notifications and remediation evidence.
clientUse: Build a data inventory and map processing to lawful bases.
Review DPIAs, retention and data-subject request operations.
Audit processor contracts and transfer mechanisms.
Connect privacy evidence to ISO 27701 and information-security controls.

frameworks.title: NIST Privacy Framework 1.0
frameworks.hook: Manage privacy risk as a business outcome, not just a compliance tick.
frameworks.summary: The NIST Privacy Framework is a voluntary tool for managing privacy risk while enabling data use. Its functions help organizations identify data processing, govern privacy, control risk and communicate with stakeholders.
keyPoints: Five functions: Identify-P, Govern-P, Control-P, Communicate-P and Protect-P.
Focuses on privacy risk arising from data processing, not only security compromise.
Profiles describe current and target privacy outcomes for a product or enterprise.
The framework is designed to work alongside the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
It covers the data-processing ecosystem, including partners and third parties.
It does not replace GDPR or sector privacy laws; it provides an operating structure.
crownJewels: Personal data and sensitive data flows across the processing ecosystem.

Lawful-basis and consent records.
Retention, deletion and data-subject request evidence.

frameworks.title: NIST SP 800-88: Media Sanitization

Crypto-erase depends on key destruction and key-management evidence.

Data-bearing devices leaving the organization.

frameworks.title: PCI DSS v4.0.1

Scope reduction through segmentation, tokenization and P2PE is a core strategy.
Compliance is validated through SAQs or a QSA assessment depending on volume and model.

The cardholder data environment and its connected systems.
Encryption keys, key-management processes and HSMs.
Payment terminals, e-commerce scripts and payment applications.
Access, monitoring and audit logs across the CDE.

frameworks.title: PCI 3-D Secure (3DS)
frameworks.hook: Security requirements for the authentication layer behind card-not-present payments.

Access to 3DS systems should follow least privilege and strong authentication.

Third-party 3DS providers extend the compliance and assurance boundary.

One-time passwords and risk-based authentication decisions.
Cryptographic keys and secure channels between 3DS components.

frameworks.title: PCI PIN Security

Key generation, distribution, rotation and destruction need dual control and split knowledge.
HSMs and key-injection facilities are high-value assets requiring physical and logical protection.

Weak key management and unmanaged terminals are recurring causes of PIN compromise.

Terminal and HSM cryptographic keys.
Key-injection facilities and key-loading processes.
POS and ATM terminals in the field.

frameworks.title: SWIFT Customer Security Programme (CSP)

Payment fraud, insider misuse and compromised operator credentials are core threat scenarios.
Third-party service providers and local middleware extend the risk boundary.

Operator credentials, tokens and privileged access.

Risk assessments and asset inventories drive control selection.

Security levels SL1 to SL4 describe resistance to increasingly capable attackers.

frameworks.title: ISO/IEC 22301:2019 Business Continuity
frameworks.hook: The certifiable management system for surviving disruption.
frameworks.summary: ISO/IEC 22301 specifies requirements for a business continuity management system (BCMS). It helps organizations understand critical services, set recovery objectives and maintain plans that work under real disruption.
keyPoints: Business impact analysis identifies critical products, services and dependencies.
Recovery time objectives, recovery point objectives and minimum service levels drive strategy.
Continuity strategies address people, facilities, technology, suppliers and communications.
Plans must be exercised, evaluated and improved, not just documented.
Leadership, risk assessment and performance evaluation are integral to the management system.
The standard can be certified and integrates with ISO 27001 and ISO 31000.
Crisis management, warnings and communication are explicit requirements.

frameworks.title: NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
frameworks.hook: Start the migration before quantum computers can harvest today's secrets.
frameworks.summary: NIST's first post-quantum cryptography standards define algorithms for key establishment and digital signatures. They give organizations a path to replace vulnerable public-key cryptography before large-scale quantum computers arrive.
keyPoints: FIPS 203 specifies ML-KEM for key encapsulation, based on the CRYSTALS-Kyber design.
FIPS 204 specifies ML-DSA for digital signatures, based on Dilithium.
FIPS 205 specifies SLH-DSA, a hash-based signature scheme for different trust assumptions.
The migration affects TLS, VPNs, PKI, code signing, firmware and long-lived data protection.
Harvest-now-decrypt-later makes long-lived confidentiality data a near-term priority.
Crypto agility, inventory and hybrid deployments are practical first steps.
NIST transition guidance and additional signature standards continue to evolve.
